title: The Complete Czech Republic Travel Guide
subtitle: Fairy-tale castles, spa towns and a beer culture built into daily life, across Bohemia and Moravia
summary: How to plan a Czech Republic trip: whether to focus on Prague, Bohemia or Moravia, when to go for the best weather and crowds, what it costs, and a practical nine-day itinerary.

sections.title: How the Czech Republic divides
body: The Czech Republic divides into three distinct parts — Prague, the rest of Bohemia, and Moravia — and a first trip realistically covers the first two well.
**Prague.** The capital and the country's single biggest draw, easily worth three or four days alone.

**Bohemia beyond Prague.** [[cesky-krumlov|Český Krumlov]], [[kutna-hora|Kutná Hora]], [[karlovy-vary|Karlovy Vary]], [[plzen|Plzeň]] and [[bohemian-switzerland|Bohemian Switzerland]] — fairy-tale towns, a grand spa resort, the home of pilsner and dramatic sandstone scenery, all within easy reach of the capital.
**Moravia.** [[brno|Brno]], [[telc|Telč]], [[lednice-valtice|Lednice-Valtice]] and [[olomouc|Olomouc]] — the quieter, wine-producing east, with its own dialect and a noticeably slower pace.
sections.note: Most first-time visitors spend the bulk of their trip in Prague and Bohemia. Moravia is where a longer or second trip belongs, and it rewards the extra travel time.

list.title: If this is your first trip
list.text: [[prague|Prague]] and a couple of easy day trips to [[kutna-hora|Kutná Hora]] or [[cesky-krumlov|Český Krumlov]], the classic starting point.

list.title: If you want a fairy-tale old town
list.text: [[cesky-krumlov|Český Krumlov]] or [[telc|Telč]], two of Central Europe's best-preserved historic towns.

list.title: If you want to relax at a spa
list.text: [[karlovy-vary|Karlovy Vary]], the grandest of Bohemia's 19th-century spa towns.

list.title: If you're a beer enthusiast
list.text: [[plzen|Plzeň]], the birthplace of pilsner, home to the original Pilsner Urquell brewery.

list.title: If you want dramatic nature
list.text: [[bohemian-switzerland|Bohemian Switzerland]], a landscape of sandstone towers and deep gorges near the German border.

list.title: If you want wine country and a slower pace
list.text: [[brno|Brno]], [[lednice-valtice|Lednice-Valtice]] and [[olomouc|Olomouc]] in Moravia, Czech travel with far fewer international visitors.

sections.title: Getting around: trains, buses, and one common mistake
body: The Czech Republic's compact size and excellent rail network mean trains and buses cover almost the entire country comfortably.
**Take the train between major cities.** [[prague|Prague]] to [[brno|Brno]] or [[olomouc|Olomouc]] runs frequently, comfortably and cheaply by Czech rail or RegioJet.
**Don't try to see Bohemia and Moravia in a rushed loop.** The most common planning mistake — Moravia deserves at least two or three unhurried days, not a single rushed day trip from Prague.

**Rent a car for Bohemian Switzerland and the wine country.** [[bohemian-switzerland|Bohemian Switzerland]] and [[lednice-valtice|Lednice-Valtice]]'s villages are far easier to explore with your own wheels.
**Use organised day trips sparingly.** [[kutna-hora|Kutná Hora]] and [[cesky-krumlov|Český Krumlov]] are both reachable by direct train or bus, often cheaper and just as easy as a group tour.
sections.note: Validate every train and bus ticket before boarding, and keep it until you leave the station — Czech ticket inspectors do check, and fines for an unvalidated ticket are steep.

sections.title: When to go
body: The Czech Republic has a distinct case for each season, though **May, June and September** offer the best overall balance.
**Late spring and early autumn** bring mild temperatures and thinner crowds, the sweet spot for most itineraries.
**Summer** is warm and lively, with long evenings on beer garden terraces, though central Prague gets crowded and accommodation prices peak.
**Winter**, especially December, is magical around Christmas markets and snow-dusted spires, though days are short and some rural attractions reduce their hours.
sections.note: Book Prague accommodation well ahead for the December Christmas market season and for any summer weekend — both sell out the best-located options early.

list.title: Four days: Prague alone
list.text: [[prague|Prague]] at an unhurried pace, enough time for the castle, Old Town and a single day trip.
list.tip: Buy a multi-day public transport pass — you'll use it more than you expect.

list.title: Nine days: the classic Bohemia and Moravia loop
list.text: The itinerary on the [[c:czech-republic|Czech Republic country page]]: [[prague|Prague]], [[kutna-hora|Kutná Hora]], [[cesky-krumlov|Český Krumlov]], [[karlovy-vary|Karlovy Vary]], [[brno|Brno]] and [[lednice-valtice|Lednice-Valtice]]. A complete first look at both regions.
list.tip: Book Český Krumlov Castle's interior tour ahead in summer — time slots do sell out.

list.title: A week focused on Bohemia
list.text: [[prague|Prague]], [[kutna-hora|Kutná Hora]], [[cesky-krumlov|Český Krumlov]], [[karlovy-vary|Karlovy Vary]] and [[plzen|Plzeň]], skipping Moravia entirely.
list.tip: This route keeps travel times short, ideal for a first trip without a car.

list.title: A slower Moravia add-on for a second trip
list.text: [[brno|Brno]], [[telc|Telč]], [[lednice-valtice|Lednice-Valtice]] and [[olomouc|Olomouc]], the region most international visitors skip entirely.
list.tip: Rent a bicycle around Lednice-Valtice — the wine trails are built for cycling between villages.

faq.q: How many days do you need in the Czech Republic?
faq.a: Seven to ten days covers Prague plus Bohemia and a taste of Moravia, which is the itinerary in this guide. Four days is enough for Prague alone.

faq.q: Is Prague worth visiting if it's crowded?
faq.a: Yes — its Old Town and castle district earn the crowds, and visiting the castle early morning or staying an extra day to explore beyond the main sights both help.

faq.q: Do you need to speak Czech to travel there?
faq.a: No, not in Prague and other tourist areas, though a few basic phrases go a long way in smaller Bohemian and Moravian towns.

faq.q: Is Moravia worth the extra travel time?
faq.a: Yes, for a second trip especially — its wine country, historic towns and noticeably fewer crowds make it feel like a different, quieter Czech Republic.
